en: *The Sūtra of the Great General of Ghosts Aṭavaka’s Superior Buddha-Dhāraṇī*, one fascicle;
also simply titled *The Aṭavaka Dhāraṇī Sūtra*.
Translated during the Liang dynasty (lost), verified by Yuanjue; Xiao Zhen.
Thus have I heard.
At one time the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha in the Kalandakanivāpa of the Bamboo Grove.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu within the city of Rājagṛha.
They will be plundered by bandits,
bitten by snakes,
and tormented by ghosts.
He experienced great suffering and distress.
At that time, the great general of the spirits, Aṭavaka, seeing this bhikṣu undergoing such suffering, felt compassion in his heart.
He immediately went to where the Buddha was, and having arrived at the Buddha's presence...
He prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, stood to one side,
and addressed the Buddha, saying: “World-Honored One,
[I have come] to subdue all the most wicked spirits and demons.”
Out of compassion for all sentient beings,
and for the purpose of subduing all malevolent spirits, ghosts, demons, and the poisons of all wicked people,
I now offer this most formidable and terrible incantation to the World-Honored Buddha.
By means of this, one subdues all spirits and deities.
If there be anyone who reads and recites this mantra,
that person’s majestic virtue and power shall even be able to subdue the Brahmā Heaven.
How much more so for other evils?
At that time, the Buddha said to the great general of spirits, Aṭavaka:
"I do not comply with this most evil and fierce incantation."
"If they might harm various sentient beings," at that time Aṭavaka addressed the Buddha again, saying, "World-Honored One,
in future ages evil spirits will increase and flourish."
There are many wicked people and venomous insects and beasts that afflict sentient beings.
Or they may encounter various calamities,
namely the perils of kings, thieves, water, fire, weapons, fear, enmity, and malevolent spirits.
Whether they be disciples of the Buddha who have gone forth or remain at home,
whether they practice dwelling in tranquility, begging for food,
or frequenting roads, cemeteries, or beneath trees— these constitute the fourfold assembly and so forth.
Whether traveling through wildernesses, mountain forests, or on roads,
or whether in cities, towns, villages, or streets, may you provide protection so that we do not encounter evil.
World-Honored One, out of your compassionate pity, we pray that you will graciously accept us.
"O World-Honored One, the Well-Gone One, we pray that you will deign to look upon us and accept us.
At that time, having heard these words, the World-Honored One accepted them by remaining silent.
Then, seeing the Buddha’s silence, Aṭavaka felt great joy in his heart.
Then, before the Buddha, he spoke this mantra:
*tuṅgie tuṅgie dāmie dāmie tuḷue tuḷue tuḷue tuḷue tuḷue tuḷue liṇi liṇi liṇi nare nare nare liṇi liṇi liṇi nara nuviṇi li tuḷu tuḷu ḍaṅgi ḍaṅgi mahātuḷu ḍaṅgi kuṭaṅgi kuṭaṅgi mahākuṭaṅgi*
Cūḍa ṭaṅga ṭaṅga ṭaṅga mahā-ṭaṅga ṭaṅga ṭaṭa ṭaṭa ṭaṭa ṭaṭa ṭaṭa mahā-ṭaṭa ṭaṭa ṭaṭa ṭaṭa abhi abhi mahā-abhi abhi abhi abhi-ri abhi-ri āpa āpa bhi-bhi mahā-āpa-bhi āpa-bhi.
Vīra vīra riṅga riṅga riṅga mahā-vīra vīra.
Liling liling mahāling ling ślu ślu.
Mahāśūlu śūlu kulu kulu mahākulu kulu luku mu luku mu.
Liú chóu liú chóu móu móu chóu mó chóu mó chóu mó chóu mó.
He li he li he li he li | yi chi yi chi yi chi yi chi | bi chi bi chi bi chi bi chi |
Halahala halahala khe ni khe ni khe ni khe ni khū ni khū ni khū ni khū ni.
He ni he ni ha na ha na ha na ha na muni muni muni muni.
Mahāmuni muni vara vara vara varāṇī li kṣuṇa ruka cāri se se (one manuscript reads *śe* hereafter).

At that time, at that moment, at that instant, [the mantra is recited]: *tadyathā | tathā | tadā | naivāna-muśe-sukā-tudatā-munika-rāma-kārama-kārama-kārama-ja-kṣeti-ta-śe-śamatha-ma-śamatha-ma-yamatha-ma-yamatha-ma-śama-muditā-miti-nā-bharāja-śanā-me-puruṣa-ma-munina-vi-jñā-mi-sukā-tudatā-munina-vi-jñā-me svāhā*. World-Honored One, these are the phrases of this dhāraṇī.
Acting as a savior for all sentient beings,
they shall protect and sustain these people, causing them all to attain peace, tranquility,
and freedom from decline and affliction.
It extinguishes all evil poisons and brings liberation from all suffering and affliction—
the perils of kings, the perils of bandits, and the perils of enmity and hatred.
Whether it be devas, nāgas, ghosts, spirits, rākṣasas, yakṣas, kumbhāṇḍas, pūtanas, āpasmāras, or khaṭvāṅgas.
In this way, all those who are afflicted or harmed shall have their suffering entirely extinguished.
Furthermore, regarding all poisons in the world—
whether from grass, wood, roots, flowers, fruits, clothing, food, drink, or any other worldly things— [they shall likewise be neutralized].
Furthermore, may all insects, birds, beasts, and nāgas that are poisonous, malevolent,
or harmful to humans be completely neutralized and rendered incapable of doing evil;
likewise, may this apply to those in the void, the sun, moon, and stars, the whirlwind wind-circles, and the ghosts and spirits.
May the various spirits and deities who arise with the intent to harm humans,
those who come seeking food to suck the vital essence of people, and those who afflict the face with disease,
fever, or illnesses lasting one day, two days, three days, four days, or even up to seven days— [may they be subdued].
Whether it be diseases of cold, wind, dampness, or heat; or any of the various ailments,
both internal and external, within the body—
whether for seven days or sixteen days.
They shall all be completely extinguished so that they cannot cause harm.
As for these various spirits and ghosts,
whether with their hands or their feet—
If one wishes to afflict others with the tongue or the mind,
or if a wicked person intends to cause harm to another,
this mantra should first be recited; its power is able to restrain them.
"May those evil persons and evil spirits be silenced, crushed, and deprived of their mindfulness, so that they do not commit evil.
World-Honored One, I shall now recite a divine mantra to protect them.
He then spoke the mantra:

Acche acche cchami muni muni mahāmuni muni uṇi hu hu mahānāga hu hu ḍgana chi āhu āganachi ādana āṭha āṭha āṭhanaṭha naṭha. Rudu rudu. Rudu huhududu. Ruhe nihe nihe nihe nihe. Ucu mu cu mu cu mu cu mu he li he li he li he li. Nili nili mahānili svāhā. This is the dhāraṇī.
I shall provide protection for those who uphold, read, and recite [this teaching].
Should there be spirits that consume the vital essence of humans,
or those that exhaust people's assets and plunder their wealth;
In this way, all fears, enemies, and the like are entirely bound within the protective boundary (*sīmābandha*).
Now, for such-and-so person and their entire household,
I perform immeasurable and great protection.
Now I shall further repeat the recitation for the prevention of all evils.
Thus he spoke the mantra:

*Lu-mu lu-mu lu-mo lu-mo lu-mo xi-li xi-li xi-li xi-li xi-li qiu-na qiu-na qiu-na qiu-na qiu-na qiu-na qiu-tu qiu-tu qiu-tu qiu-lu qiu-lu qiu-lu qiu-lu xiu-lou xiu-lou xiu-lou xiu-lou xiu-lou xi-li-mu xiu-mu xi-li-mu xi-li-mu xi-li-mu xi-li xiu-mou xiu-mou xiu-mou xiu-mo xiu-mie ti-mo-mie si-mo-a-ti-ga-la-mie-er-she-huo.* The Great General addressed the Buddha once more, saying:
World-Honored One, this mantra possesses the supreme spiritual power as described above.
May those who uphold this mantra have no fear of kings, no fear of thieves, no fear of fire, no fear of water,
no fear of wind-poisons, and no fear of weapons or warfare.
The sun, moon, stars, and spirits fear it;
or there may be other evil associates who give rise to anger and jealousy in their hearts.
If there are those who harbor malicious intent, seeking to harm or invade with affliction,
one should first recite this mantra to establish a boundary for them.
This shall cause those evil spirits, wicked persons, or enemies whose minds give rise to malice and aggression to turn back.
It shall cause them to become deluded, fainting and crushed;
encountering various evils themselves,
they shall not transcend this realm and shall be unable to invade or harm those who recite this mantra.
World-Honored One, if there are good sons or good daughters who recite this mantra,
all devas, nāgas, asuras, and various evil ghosts and spirits— whether human or non-human— [shall be subdued].
"We shall all attend upon and protect you, ensuring that no evil befalls you.
World-Honored One, I am a great general of ghosts and spirits;
my power is able to subdue all demons."
If there be anyone who recites this mantra,
I shall lead all the spirits and deities to protect that person day and night without departing,
ensuring that evil spirits or wicked people find no opportunity to harm them.
If anyone should violate, damage, afflict, or harm those who recite this mantra,
I shall crush their heads with a thousand-spoked wheel and cause all the ghosts and spirits to bring them ruin and harm.
"Blessed One, this mantra possesses supreme spiritual power and supreme majesty.
We pray only that it may be disseminated for the peace and happiness of all beings.
Blessed One, those who recite this mantra—"
The power of that person’s virtue is known only to the Buddha.
This great divine mantra should be entrusted to those who are worthy and wise.
If one is unable to recite it, [it should not be given].
One should write it on high-quality paper, place it in a multicolored silk pouch, and,
having applied various kinds of incense, constantly carry it with one's person.
Should there be any anxiety, fear, or impending danger, [one should recite it].
One should always keep this mantra in mind; there is nothing it cannot eliminate.
World-Honored One, if there are difficult circumstances, anxieties, fears, malevolent spirits, evil ghosts, or nightmares that one wishes to have extinguished, [one should recite this].
First, one should establish a boundary so that no evils may arise.
This shall cause those wicked people, evil spirits,
and malevolent thieves to suffer their own calamities— their bodies withered and parched, and their minds deranged— at the very moment the boundary is being established.
One should bathe and purify oneself, put on clean garments, and thoroughly cleanse the ground.
One should arrange seven vessels for various drinks;

two vessels should contain a small amount of blood, and one vessel should contain various kinds of beverages. Then, light eight lamps, burn incense of *guggulu*, and perform the offering with a focused mind.
I shall lead all the spirits and deities to that person’s side to grant their wishes.
That person should recite this mantra and tie a red thread, and then carry it with them;
they will immediately be able to eliminate all calamities.
At that time, the Buddha told Ānanda:
"This mantra possesses exceedingly great supernatural power;
it can eliminate all evils and protect sentient beings."
It brings great benefit.
You should receive and uphold it well, and cause it to be widely disseminated.
In any city, town, or village where this mantra is recited, there shall be no lack of benefit.
If there are kings or ministers who recite this mantra,
their realm shall be free from the terrors of evil bandits, calamities, misfortunes, epidemics, droughts, floods, wind, and frost.
If one encounters wicked bandits, one should recite this mantra.
If it is fastened atop a high banner,
when the bandits see this banner, they will immediately retreat and disperse, being brought to submission.
"Ānanda, this dhāraṇī possesses supreme spiritual power and immense majesty.
You should cause the fourfold assembly to skillfully recite and uphold it.
At that time, the assembled multitude, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
If one practices this rite,
first paint a single panel of the Great Powerful General Ganesha upon a piece of the finest silk,
whether it be one, three, or four panels in size.
Begin painting on the first day of the eighth month.
Whether painting it yourself or instructing others to paint it, both are permissible.
First, observe the seven-day fast.
He then donned exquisite, superior garments and performed a pure ablution.
He then received the eight precepts from the painter.
In a clean room, he hung banners and flowers.
Construct a great fire altar one foot high;
upon the altar, place an abundance of hard charcoal embers.
Then, take white-juice wood and cut it into one thousand and eight pieces.
Take sesame seeds, non-glutinous rice, honey, curd, and fragrant flowers;
recite the mantra once for each item as you burn them all.
Once the materials are exhausted, use excellent, superior colors.
Recite the mantra one hundred and eight times over the altar.
Do not use glue as an adhesive;
instead, take the sap of the śveta-śāla tree and mix it with the resin of incense (guggulu).
Once after using the toilet and once after bathing,
one should paint the General Aṭavaka,
who is blackish-blue in color, six feet tall, and has four faces.
The front face is that of a Buddha;
the left face has crossed fangs and three eyes,
with eyes as red as blood.
The right face is that of a deity,
with a wrathful expression, bared fangs, and three eyes;
it has fangs and hair extending to the left and right.
Upon his head, one face displays a wrathful expression;
it also has three eyes and fangs, with eyes protruding and red as the color of blood.
The hair on the uppermost head is entwined by a red dragon.
Flames rise continuously from the crown of his head;
he wears snake-earrings and a snake coiled around his neck,
and possesses eight arms.
The upper left hand holds a wheel;
the second [left] hand holds a spear;
the third [left] hand and the third right hand [are joined].
Now, perform the offering mudrā:
hold a noose with the lower left hand and a vajra with the upper right hand.
The second hand holds a staff;
the third hand forms the *viśvavajra* mudrā;
the lower hand holds a sword.
His fingers, wrists, and upper arms were all entwined by snakes;
his body was clad in armor interlaced with the seven treasures,
and his shoulders were covered entirely by dragons.
The nāga is joined together and hangs down from the chest;
it emerges with three faces, two of which have red and yellow eyes and their mouths closed.
The faces to its left and right above are both dark blue and deep in color.
The upper part is yellowish-white;
the left side is white; the right side is reddish-black;
and the front is bluish-white.
His hands are all blue; he wears an elephant hide as a turban, and his feet wear sandals.
His feet trample two yakṣas, both of which are black.
The deity manifests an extremely fierce appearance;
his formidable and majestic form is as previously described, acting with great vigor.
To his left and right, four attendants are depicted.
On the left are Dhṛtarāṣṭra and Virūḍhaka;
on the right are Virūpākṣa and Vaiśravaṇa—
all of whom display expressions of wrath.
He wears a crown of the seven precious gems and is clad in fine golden armor;
his arms are adorned with bracelets shaped like dragon heads, and he is draped in celestial robes, bound by bands of the seven precious gems, and wearing sandals.
He treads upon yakṣas with his feet.
The same applies to the right side as well.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra holds a sword to press down upon it,
and Virūḍhaka holds a trident.
Virūpākṣa brandishes a sword;
Vaiśravaṇa wields a mace;
the Four Heavenly Kings each lead their retinues.
The Heavenly King of the East leads the Gandharva generals and holds a bell-tassel;
the Heavenly King of the South leads the Kumbhāṇḍa kings and holds a bow and arrow;
the Heavenly King of the West leads the Nāga kings and holds a sword.
The Northern Heavenly King, the Yakṣa King who wields the subduing *tuṅ*,
has clouds of crimson-black rising above his head.
Beneath the feet of the Four Heavenly Kings, two youths dressed in blue garments are fashioned.
Holding a paper and a brush in the right hand and an inkstone tray in the left,
one should fashion a single *tengai* (heavenly crown) before the deity to serve as an incense burner for offering.
It must be made with the utmost freshness and cleanliness.
One's desires will be fulfilled as wished.
If one wishes to seek a vision of a deity,
[one should do so] on the seventh day of the seventh month or the third day of the third month.
Gather all grasses, trees, flowers, rice, grains, flowers, ghee, honey, and curd, and burn them.
When all the heavenly deities and the eight classes of beings see this,
they will all rejoice and manifest their forms.
If one is subduing a great Māra or a deity, one should sit with the legs suspended.
With both hands, one should tightly form fists and press them down upon the two thighs.
Immediately bite the lower lip with the upper lip and look with wide-open eyes;
this is the Great Subjugation Seal (Mahāvaśīkaraṇamudrā). First, as for the seal for binding spirits and demons:
interlace the two little fingers of the left and right hands in a reversed manner.
Press the two thumbs upon the tips of the two little fingers;
extend the middle and ring fingers upright, and do the same for the index fingers.
Second, this is the Seal for Commanding Ghosts and Spirits.
Sit in the *paryaṅka* (half-lotus) posture, supporting the hip with the left hand.
With the right hand, press the thumb upon the nails of the ring finger and little finger.
Straighten and point upward the index and middle fingers. Thirdly, if subduing powerful malevolent spirits, perform the *Agnicakra-mudrā* (Fire-Wheel Seal).
Bend the two ring fingers of both hands within the palms so that their tips are aligned;
let the remaining fingers support one another with their tips slightly separated from the palms—this is the fourth [mudrā].
If one wishes to cast out possessing spirits (bhūta-grahas), [one should employ this mudrā].
To form the mudrā, interlace the three fingers below the middle fingers behind the back of the palms;
join the two index fingers together so that they are level.
Cross the thumb over the two fingers and press upon the middle joint of the second finger.
Recite three times and breathe three times; thus one binds [the spirits] and brings them forth. The above five kinds of ritual mudrās (*mudrā*) employ the Great Mantra.
The mantra for the Four Heavenly Kings to bind the boundaries (*sīmābandha*) is as follows:

Oṃ sādhye bhaṇḍa bhaṇḍa haṃ hūṃ phaṭ. [For] all eight classes of spirits: Namo buddhāya, namo dharmāya, namaḥ saṃghāya; namo bhūriyakṣebhyaḥ, kailāsayakṣebhyaḥ, devīryakṣebhyaḥ, aṭapakoṭubhyo svāhā. If one pursues the eight classes of deities, raise the aforementioned mudrās of the eight classes.
He immediately recited the aforementioned mantra twenty-one times.
That deity arrived instantly, saying, "World-Honored One, I pray that you cause this to be transmitted and spread throughout Jambudvīpa."
May all sentient beings uphold this,
so that it may serve as their great protection. Aṭṭhapuṭa.
There are seventy-two chief generals who command ghosts and spirits;
there are thirty-two great deity-kings and twenty-eight ghost-kings.
Each king leads a retinue of twenty-five thousand followers.
He constantly attends and serves as a vanguard for the Great General.
If any human or spirit hears the name of this great deity,
or if the Great General becomes angry, one should recite the name of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva one hundred and eight times.
If various ghosts and spirits become angry, one should immediately take a handful of ashes and scatter them toward their mouths to establish a small boundary;
by maintaining this practice, one can cure diseases.
According to the ritual procedures of the Peacock King:
if one wishes to see spirits and deities,
one should collect piglets on the seventh day of the seventh lunar month.
If one wears [the image] for twenty-one days, one will immediately see [him].
Next is the method of Aṭavaka:
using twelve arrows, two swords, and forty-nine lamps.
Place ghee, milk, honey, and syrup each in separate vessels;
prepare two mirrors and consecrate white mustard seeds with mantras.
One scatters [grain] at the four corners to establish the boundary field (*sīmā*).
It is not with threads or cords that one establishes the mantra-boundary (*mantra-sīmā*).
[The materials used are] willow branches, peach branches, hot water, reeds, and fire.
Then, using the celestial net,
one recites the seal-mantra three times and ties twelve knots.

1. The Request for the Dharma of the Worthy and Holy Ones by Aṭavaka. Chapter One: Requesting the Seal of the Buddhas of the Ten Directions. First, recite the seal of the Buddhas of the ten directions eight times: *Oṃ jaya-pāhe svāhā*. (Note: *pāhe* is read as *yū-ā-fǎn*).
Interlace the two ring fingers of the left and right hands within the palms.
Straighten the two middle fingers so that their tips touch one another.
Bend the two index fingers to press down upon the backs of the proximal joints of the middle fingers.
Simultaneously extend both thumbs and press against the sides of their middle joints;
move the index fingers back and forth seven times,
and immediately all Buddhas will arrive.
2. The Seal for Invoking Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva. Second: Oṃ viśuddhe vijayamati lokaviśaye svāhā. Join the two wrists together.
The two thumbs are placed side by side;
the two little fingers are likewise.
The remaining fingers are slightly spread, slightly curved, and held upright like a lotus bud.
The index fingers move up and down. 3.
The Mudrā for Summoning the Vajras of the Fourteen Divisions: Recite "Oṃ vajra-āvartani he svāhā. With both forearms extended sideways, join the two thumbs together.
Twist each [finger] over its respective small fingernail.
The two ring fingers are held upright on their sides, touching at their tips.
The two middle fingers are each held straight and upright.
The tips [of the thumbs] face forward and do not touch.
Move the two index fingers back and forth. 4.
The Seal for Assembling the Thirty-three Heavenly Deities. The Seal for Assembling the Thirty-three Heavenly Deities (4): Oṃ śloka rūpa-lama-dhāniye svāhā. (2) (2) Insert the ring fingers within.
Place the two middle fingers together.
Extend the two index fingers so that their backs rest against the middle of the two middle fingers.
Slightly separate the two index fingers from the second joints of the middle fingers.
Approximately half [the size].
Move the thumb back and forth. 5.

*Ji-er-shi-ba-xiu-xing-tian-yin* (Collection of the Celestial Seals of the Twenty-eight Lunar Mansions). Five: Oṃ tārā devatāye svāhā. With the left hand, place the middle and ring fingers together, palms facing upward.
Place the right middle finger above the lower joint of the left ring finger;
likewise, place the right ring finger covered over the lower joint of the left middle finger.
In its entirety, the fingers are interlaced like a rope.
The little fingers, index fingers, and thumbs are each extended and pressed together;
the thumbs move back and forth.

(6) This is the seal for the Eastern Heavenly King Dhṛtarāṣṭra, who leads the hosts of gandharvas. [Mantra: Oṃ dhṛtidi-hara-śeṭha yakṣa indra-rāja bhadre svāhā. With the left hand, the three fingers below the middle finger are clenched into a fist.
Furthermore, bend the index finger slightly and place it upon the joint of the lower phalanx of the middle finger;
then move the thumb back and forth.
7. The Seal for Summoning the Southern Heavenly King Virūḍhaka and His Host of Kumbhāṇḍas: Seven times: Oṃ virūḍhakāśipadaye svāhā. [Place it] at the left wrist.
Place the side of the right wrist upon the base of the left wrist.
With the two palms facing away from each other,
hook the two ring fingers and the two middle fingers together and extend them like a rope.
The two little fingers and the two index fingers, along with the two thumbs, are each slightly bent.
The index fingers move back and forth. 8.

The Seal for Summoning the Western Vajrapāṇi Heavenly King and His Dragon Army. The seal for summoning the Western Vajrapāṇi Heavenly King and his dragon army is: Oṃ bilu vajra kumbhāṇḍa dīpate svāhā. [Hold] the left hand at the side of the forearm.
Place the right wrist upon the base of the left wrist.
As for the three fingers from the middle finger downward on both hands,
each is bent into the palm to form fists.
Bend the two thumbs and press them against the top [of the hands];
interlace the two index fingers like a cord or a gauntlet,
while the thumbs move back and forth.
9. Seal for Summoning Vaiśravaṇa, King of the Northern Quarter, Who Leads the Yakṣa Armies. [Seal No. 9]: Oṃ vaiśravaṇāya ādhipataye svāhā. [Mudrā: The right forearm.
Furthermore, bend the index finger and the four fingers below it against the palm to form a fist;
bend the thumb and press it down upon the index finger.
Do the same with the right wrist.
Forming fists at the sides,
extend the thumbs straight upward;
place the right fist stacked upon the left hand.
Move the right thumb back and forth. 10.

The Seal for Assembling the Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, and the Eight Classes of Ghost-Soldiers of the Four Heavenly Kings under Their Command. The Seal for Assembling the Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, and the Eight Classes of Ghost-Soldiers of the Four Heavenly Kings under Their Command (10): *Oṃ cāṇḍāla śrīdharāya svāhā*. Reverse the index fingers and middle fingers, inserting them into the palms.
The ring fingers are held upright with their tips touching;
the two little fingers are crossed at their upper joints so that they are level,
while the hands are brought together with the palms joined at the wrists.
The thumb moves back and forth. 11.

The Seal for Assembling the Hosts of the Eight Classes of Nāga Kings. The Seal for Assembling the Hosts of the Eight Classes of Nāga Kings, Number Eleven: Oṃ Upananda Svāhā. Place the right elbow inside the left elbow.
Again, with the right hand, slightly curve the last four fingers;
with the thumb, touch the index finger which is also slightly curved.
Reverse the left hand to face the right hand, performing the same action.
It resembles the mouth of a snake and is used as follows:
the four fingers of each of the two hands move back and forth. 12.
The Seal of the Dragon King Who Pursues Hundreds of Thousands of Deva-Nāgas to Raise Clouds and Send Down Rain. 12. Oṃ Bhu-kīra Svāhā. The left and right arms and wrists remain as before, unchanged.
Simply take the little fingers and ring fingers of both hands,
cross them with the right over the left so they enter the palms,
and extend the two middle fingers straight upward with their tips touching.
The two index fingers rest upon the upper joints of the middle fingers;
the two thumbs are slightly curved,
each resting upon the inner middle joints of the two index fingers.
Moving the index fingers back and forth. 13.

The Seal for Pursuing the Army of the Sun Deity (Sūryadevatā). The seal for pursuing the army of the Sun Deity, number thirteen: Oṃ raśmi-mārīṇi svāhā. First, turn the backs of the two middle fingers, ring fingers, and little fingers [toward each other].
The palms are pressed together so that they are level;
the two index fingers are held straight and vertical against each other,
while the two thumbs press upon the first joints at the bases of the index fingers.
The thumb moves back and forth. 14.

It subdues all externalists and spirits, none of whom dare to oppose it.
When ghosts see the practitioner, they perceive him as no different from themselves.
One should recite the mantra over a stone, a finger, or a branch once.
He pressed down upon it with his hand.
When the ghost saw this sword,
the sorcerer who subdues demons did not inquire as to how great the person's mental power might be.
They drew lines on the ground to encircle him, and he was completely bound;
weeping, he spoke these words:
"The spells of the heterodox afflict all people, making them difficult to cure."
If heavy karmic offenses from previous lives exist,
Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva shall deliver them;
Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva shall seal them with the Seal for Extirpating Transgressions.
One who treats the illness of Māra should recite the name of the Bodhisattva Amoghapāśa three times;
it will then be easily cured.
If one wishes to cure an illness in another's household,
one should pursue the Lord of the Hearth and question him;
then one will immediately know whether it will be auspicious or inauspicious.
As for the reality, it causes the Lord of the Southern Dipper to strike the seal of prohibition.
A virtuous woman shall then immediately speak of good and evil.
This applies to anyone who is ill.
Those who have faith can be cured;
those who lack faith are icchantikas,
who need not be treated as they are incurable.
If one merely sprinkles water consecrated with mantras,
the illnesses of all people will likewise be cured. Furthermore,
if a woman who has no children bathes herself with pure cleanliness, [she shall obtain offspring].
With a sincere heart, take refuge in the Triple Gem.
Recite the mantra over a single grain of white mustard seed one thousand and eight times;
by swallowing it, one shall obtain a child.
If one is my disciple,
I myself shall protect and sustain them so that no non-human being can find an opportunity to harm them;
they shall maintain a heart of reverence toward all spirits and deities.
Toward all mantra-practitioners, cultivate the mind of a brother;
always act with equanimity and do not harbor pride or arrogance.
Furthermore, toward all spirits and deities, conceive of them as virtuous spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*).
If a woman experiences difficult labor and is on the verge of death, one should tell her:
"Diyi, grant her a son; Siming, do not obstruct her."
If one ties a mantra-knot at the crown of the head and wears it, the illness will immediately be cured.
If an epidemic breaks out among cattle or horses,
recite the mantra over earth one hundred and eight times.
If one scatters [the ashes] over the body, the illness is immediately cured.
If suffering from dysuria, recite the mantra one hundred and twenty-eight times over red copper coins, boil them to extract the liquid, and drink it; the condition will be immediately cured.
If one wishes to bind a person, there is no need to laboriously employ seals.
"However, if one recites this mantra with a sincere heart, it shall bind when commanded to bind,
and strike when commanded to strike, acting in accordance with the human mind.
I have now manifested in the body of a bodhisattva for the sake of propagating and transforming the Buddha's teachings."
I assumed the form of a wrathful subduer.
I personally declared my efficacy before the Buddha,
and the Buddha immediately accepted my divine seal to carry out its function.
On that day, when it was used, Mahākrodhavajra recited the mantra for crushing demons,
and Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva recited the Pāśa (noose) mantra.
The Great Lord Maheśvara King also spoke one mantra.
Each of the four heavenly kings of the Māheśvara gods spoke five mantras for the subjugation of demons in the four directions.
Furthermore, among all the spirits, ghosts, yakṣas, rākṣasas, devas, nāgas, asuras, and vajrapāṇis,
I am the Generalissimo and Great Commander, the sovereign over all these spirits and ghosts.
At the very end of the final age of the Buddha-dharma,
you shall protect and mindfully care for sentient beings, causing them all to dwell in peace and security.
I regard the sentient beings of the trichiliocosm as if they were my only child.
I shall not allow evil spirits or heterodox deities to disturb sentient beings.
Should there be any spirits who harass or disturb the mantra-practitioner,

He commanded the Four Heavenly Kings to each lead a hundred koṭis of spirits and ghosts to surround him in front and behind.
At every place he passed through,
mountains and rivers shook and split apart, and a hundred ghosts fled in all directions.
At that time, I addressed the eight classes of gods, dragons, ghosts,
and spirits: "Send down a great rain and raise up great winds and clouds to confound and disorder heaven and earth while I am in a state of wrath."
The sun and moon lose their radiance;

That king is my subordinate;
he will not come to frighten you.
If you wish to eliminate the malevolent spirits, [act accordingly].
First, they gathered together for a meal and drink;
then he told them,

As for external objects,
if they do not depart, they must certainly be eliminated.
Furthermore, if one seeks the elixir of immortality, one must enter deep mountains and places where no people dwell.
He sat beneath a great tree for three days without rising or eating.

thus his life was brought to an end along with heaven and earth.
If one recites the mantra seven times over the waters of the great ocean and snaps one's fingers three times,

Furthermore, if one does not cure an illness...
Simply recite the mantra— whether it be tens of millions or hundreds of millions of times—
and simply give rise to a virtuous mind,
regarding all ghosts and spirits as great spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*).
If one conceives thoughts of loving-kindness and compassion toward all sentient beings with equanimity, at the end of that person's life, they will not pass through the hells;

At this time, in the second year of the Bao-li era, the twenty-ninth year of the sexagenary cycle (Ren-shen), in the twelfth month, the edition carved from woodblocks by Gu was requested and brought here by the two masters Xiao and Zhen. What is regrettable is that because the original master copy could not be obtained, errors have been transmitted through successive transcriptions and cannot be verified; I hope that future scholars will correct them.
